mappings.note: ratio of circumferences gives ratio of radii: tests that perimeter scales linearly in r, the perimeter half of the perimeter-vs-area distinction; no central angle, so not LO-1
annulus between two concentric circles is a composite region formed by subtracting one circle from another; no angle and no chord, so not LO-1 or LO-2
square minus an inscribed quadrant: circle-part combined with a polygon, the defining case of LO-3 rather than a bare sector area
area of a 240 degree sector is the whole question; the second circle is only a re-expression of that area, so the skill is sector area for a given central angle
path around a lawn is an annulus, a region built by subtracting one circle from a larger one
goes from a given AREA to the PERIMETER of the same semicircular figure; the trap is that the perimeter is arc plus diameter, exactly the LO-1 of C-7.2
circle inscribed in a square: the polygon fixes the radius, so this is a circle-and-polygon composite rather than a plain area recall
two circles in external contact with their areas added; area additivity across combined circles is LO-3, not a single sector
ring area, but the data are the two CIRCUMFERENCES, so the student must cross from perimeter to radius before the composite-area step
perimeter of a quadrant: the distractor 11 cm is the bare arc, so the point is perimeter = arc + two radii; arc length itself is LO-1
doubling the circumference quadruples the area: literally the perimeter-versus-area contrast, linear against quadratic
percentage change in the area of a whole circle; no sector, no segment, no composite and no perimeter, so no learning outcome fits and the competency is the honest level - see report, content gap
perimeter of a semicircular protractor is (pi + 2)r, not pi*r: the whole item is knowing what the perimeter of a figure with a circular part includes
sector area from r = 14 and a stated central angle of 45 degrees, the plain LO-1 computation
AREAS of two circles add to a third: R^2 = R1^2 + R2^2. Paired deliberately with the circumference twin below, which goes to C-7.2-LO-1
CIRCUMFERENCES of two circles add to a third: R = R1 + R2. Same figure as the previous item but the perimeter answer, which is the distinction C-7.2-LO-1 names
equal perimeters, unequal areas between a circle and a square: the perimeter-area distinction stated as a comparison
same equal-perimeter premise as the previous item but asks for the ratio of areas; still the perimeter-to-area crossing, not a sector
one park equal in area to two others: area additivity over combined circles, the LO-3 family, not the circumference family
square inscribed in a circle: the circle fixes the diagonal, a circle-and-polygon composite
circumferences add, so diameters add: the linear-perimeter result, deliberately different from the area twin two items earlier
areas of two circles add to a third; the answer needs 24^2 + 7^2, the quadratic behaviour, so this is the area branch not the perimeter branch
wire bent into a circle: its LENGTH becomes the circumference and the item then asks for the AREA, so it is the perimeter-to-area crossing
circumference to radius only; the circumference is the object of the question, which is the perimeter-facing outcome of this chapter
area of a circular path as pi(R^2 - r^2): an annulus, a composite of two circles, and the reason statement is that composite formula
